young.html: King Lear of ancient Britain is old and wants to rest. He decides to divide his kingdom among his three daughters, and asks each to say how much she loves him. The two eldest, Goneril and Regan, flatter him with grand words. The youngest, Cordelia, who loves him most, will not.

young.text:
CORDELIA. Nothing, my lord.
LEAR. Nothing?
CORDELIA. Nothing.
LEAR. Nothing will come of nothing: speak again.
young.author: William Shakespeare
young.ed: First printed in the First Folio
young.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

young.html: Lear is furious and sends Cordelia away. Soon the flattering daughters turn him out of their homes, and he goes out into a terrible storm with only his Fool and a few loyal friends. In the storm, the proud king learns what it is to be poor and cold, and at last he sees which daughter truly loved him.

young.html: For parents: King Lear is one of Shakespeare's saddest plays and includes a cruel scene in which Gloucester is blinded, and the deaths of Cordelia and Lear. Young readers can follow Act I (the love test) and the reunion of Lear and Cordelia (Act IV, scene 7) or a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

Love in words or deeds? Goneril and Regan say beautiful things; Cordelia says "Nothing" but loves her father. Make two lists: ways people show love with words, and ways they show it with actions. Which list is longer in your family?
young.title: Talk it over

full.html: Shakespeare wrote King Lear around 1605–1606, from the legend of a king of pre-Roman Britain told in Holinshed and an older play. He added a second family, the Earl of Gloucester and his two sons, whose story mirrors Lear's, and gave it an ending darker than any of his sources. It survives in two versions (1608 and 1623) that differ in many lines.

Lear wants to be loved in words, in public, and to keep the honor of a king without its work. Cordelia's "Love, and be silent" is an aside to herself; she will love and obey "according to my bond." Kent, who defends her, is banished too, and returns in disguise to serve Lear.

full.text:
How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is
To have a thankless child! Away, away!
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.work: King Lear, Act I, scene 4 (Lear, of Goneril)
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: Shut out by Goneril and Regan, Lear rages in the storm on the heath with his Fool, who tells him the truth in jokes, and with Edgar, Gloucester's loyal son, disguised as "Poor Tom," a beggar. Lear's mind gives way, and in his madness he sees more clearly than before: he pities the "poor naked wretches" he never thought of as king.

Gloucester, for helping Lear, is cruelly punished and loses his sight. Led by Edgar, whom he does not recognize, he learns to "see" his son's loyalty. In Act IV, Cordelia returns with an army from France, and Lear wakes in her care and knows her. In Act V, her army is defeated, Edgar defeats Edmund, Goneril and Regan destroy each other, Cordelia is killed, and Lear dies with her in his arms.

The ending so troubled audiences that from 1681 to the 1830s theaters played Nahum Tate's rewrite, in which Cordelia lives and marries Edgar. Samuel Johnson, later on this ladder, said he could hardly bear to reread the last scenes.
Reading Lear's madness as only a loss. In the storm Lear becomes kinder and wiser than he ever was on the throne. The play asks whether suffering can teach what power could not.

items: Is the world of King Lear just? Do the gods, as some characters say, care at all?
Why does Lear need to hear love spoken? Why can't Cordelia say it?
What does it mean that the Fool and the madman are the wisest people on the heath?
Is the ending a cruel accident, or does it mean something?

deep.html: Sophocles' Oedipus, earlier on this ladder, also loses his sight and learns the truth; the Book of Job asks why the good suffer. Dostoevsky's Brothers Karamazov, later, returns to fathers, children and the question of justice.

questions: Why do you think Lear believed the flattering daughters?
Cordelia could have saved herself with a few kind words. Was she right to refuse?
The Fool tells Lear the truth with jokes. Why is it sometimes easier to hear hard truths that way?
In the storm Lear thinks about poor people for the first time. What helps people understand others' troubles?
care: King Lear includes a cruel scene in which Gloucester is blinded, battles, and the deaths of Cordelia and Lear. This lesson summarizes these without detail and quotes nothing violent.
